## What social science is for {#what-are-we-doing-when-we-do-social-science}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Making **claims about the world** that could turn out to be wrong – and saying how we would know.
:::

::: {.fragment}
A claim is offered to others so that they can **check it, use it, argue with it, build on it**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Science depends on that handover, and everything that follows is about whether it works.
:::
::::

::: notes
I start with a question that is seldom asked aloud, what we are doing when we do social science. [advance] We make claims about the world that could turn out to be wrong, with some statement of how we would find out. [advance] A claim is published so that other people can check it, use it, argue with it and build on it, and a finding that nobody else can examine remains an assertion. [advance] When we ask whether social science is in trouble, then, the question is quite specific: whether that handover works, and whether someone else can pick up your finding and do anything with it.
:::

## False positives and forking paths {#three-arguments-that-made-people-nervous .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **The theory, 2005.** With small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and many teams chasing the same question, most published findings in a field can be false with nobody breaking any rules [@Ioannidis2005WhyMostPublished]
- **The demonstration, 2011.** Give researchers only the flexibility they legitimately have – which cases to drop, which covariates to keep, when to stop collecting – and a **false-positive rate of 5% becomes over 60%** [@SimmonsEtAl2011FalsePositivePsychology]
- **The subtlety, 2014.** You do not need many tests. In a **garden of forking paths**, a single test *chosen after looking at the data* already has the wrong p-value [@GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience]
:::

::: notes
Three arguments made people nervous, and I take the arguments in the order of how uncomfortable they are. Ioannidis made the theoretical case in 2005: with small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and many teams chasing the same question, most published findings in a field can be false without anybody breaking a rule. Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn then demonstrated it, showing that the flexibility which researchers legitimately have can push a false-positive rate of five per cent above sixty, and they made the point by 'showing', with real participants and real statistics, that listening to a Beatles song makes people younger. Gelman and Loken added the point that I find hardest to set aside: no long series of tests is needed, since a single test chosen after looking at the data already has the wrong p-value.
:::

## Evidence from replications and many-analysts studies {#and-then-people-counted .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **100 psychology studies**, replicated with high power and the original materials: **97%** of the originals were significant, **36%** of the replications were, and effect sizes roughly **halved** [@OpenScienceCollaboration2015EstimatingReproducibilityPsychological]
- **161 researchers, 73 teams, one hypothesis** on immigration and support for social policy: **1,253** models, and no convergence on either sign or significance [@BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Different fields and different designs. In the first, **most findings were not significant again in new samples**; in the second, **the result depended on who ran the analysis.**
:::

::: notes
Then people counted. The Open Science Collaboration replicated a hundred psychology studies with high power and the original materials. Ninety-seven per cent of the original studies had reported a significant result, thirty-six per cent of the replications did, and the effect sizes came back at about half their original size, and this is the study that carried the phrase 'replication crisis' outside methods seminars. The second study is closer to our own fields: seventy-three teams, one hypothesis about immigration and support for social policy, more than twelve hundred models between them, and no agreement on the sign, let alone the significance. [advance] In the first study most findings were not significant again in new samples, while in the second the result depended on who ran the analysis.
:::

## Incentives and questionable research practices {#it-is-not-mostly-fraud .smaller}

::: {.small}
Fraud exists, but it is rare. The mechanism behind these results is **ordinary and structural**:

- Journals reward novel, clean, significant results – so that is what gets written up
- Every analysis contains dozens of small defensible choices, and the analyst makes them while looking at the data
- Nobody publishes the twelve specifications that did not work; the reader sees one
- Data and code are usually not available, so nobody can check any of it
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Ask researchers anonymously, with an incentive to answer truthfully, and a **majority admit** to at least one of these ordinary practices [@JohnEtAl2012MeasuringPrevalenceQuestionable]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
None of these steps requires a dishonest person, so the problem cannot be fixed by hiring better people.
:::

::: notes
This is not mostly a story about fraud, which is rare and is not what these numbers measure. The mechanism is ordinary and structural. Journals want novel, clean, significant results, so that is what gets submitted. Every analysis contains dozens of small choices, each defensible on its own, which the analyst makes while looking at the data. Nobody writes up the twelve specifications that did not work, so the reader meets one path through a garden of hundreds, and the data and the code are usually unavailable, so nobody can check. [advance] John, Loewenstein and Prelec asked researchers anonymously, with a mechanism that made truthful answers worth giving, and a majority admitted to at least one of these practices. [advance] None of these steps requires a bad actor, so the problem cannot be solved by hiring better people. [pause] Suppose, then, that we gave the best people we could find the same data and the same question, and recorded what they did.
:::

## The red-card study {#twenty-nine-teams-one-question .smaller}

::: {.small}
**The question.** Are football referees more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players than to light-skinned ones?

**The data.** One dataset, sent to everyone: 2,053 players in the top divisions of England, Germany, France and Spain, the 3,147 referees they played under, and **146,028 player–referee pairs**. Skin tone rated from profile photographs by two coders who did not know the research question.

**The design.** Twenty-nine teams analysed it independently. They reviewed each other's approaches *before* anyone had seen a result, revised, and only then compared answers.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
This is the first many-analysts study. Every one since is a variation on it, including the one that this workshop works on.
:::

::: {.src}
@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne
:::

::: notes
Silberzahn and colleagues ran very nearly that experiment, in a study published in 2018, and every many-analysts study since, the one in which I took part included, varies its design. The question was whether football referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players than to light-skinned ones. Everyone received the same data: two thousand and fifty-three players in the top divisions of England, Germany, France and Spain, the more than three thousand referees under whom they had played, and a hundred and forty-six thousand player–referee pairs, with skin tone rated from profile photographs by two coders who were not told the research question. Twenty-nine teams analysed the data independently, reviewed each other's approaches before anybody had a result, revised, and only then compared answers, so that nobody could tune a method towards a number that they liked.
:::

## The twenty-nine estimates {#all-twenty-nine-side-by-side}

```{r}
#| label: silberzahn-forest
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 5.0
# Figure 3 of the paper, rebuilt from the authors' published values rather than
# reproduced as an image: every team, every interval, grouped by the response
# distribution it assumed. Colour is ours – the original is monochrome – and
# marks whether the interval excludes 1. Teams 21 and 27 have intervals running
# to 11.5 and 78.7; the published figure truncates both and asterisks them, and
# so does this.
CLIP <- 3.2
szf <- silberzahn29 |>
  dplyr::mutate(hi_draw = pmin(or_hi, CLIP),
         lab = paste0(team, ". ", tidy_approach(approach))) |>
  dplyr::arrange(distribution, or) |>
  dplyr::mutate(lab = factor(lab, levels = rev(lab)))

ggplot2::ggplot(szf, ggplot2::aes(or, lab, colour = significant)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "longdash", colour = grey_mid) +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbarh(ggplot2::aes(xmin = or_lo, xmax = hi_draw), height = 0, linewidth = 0.55) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(data = dplyr::filter(szf, or_hi > CLIP), ggplot2::aes(x = CLIP + 0.04, label = "*"),
            size = 5, vjust = 0.75, show.legend = FALSE) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = ncl_blue, `FALSE` = d_red),
                      breaks = c("TRUE", "FALSE"), name = NULL,
                      labels = c("interval excludes 1", "interval includes 1")) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3),
                     expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.03))) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.42, CLIP + 0.1)) +
  ggplot2::facet_grid(distribution ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "odds ratio", y = NULL,
       caption = paste("Above 1: dark-skinned players red-carded more often.",
                       "* interval runs past the edge (teams 21 and 27).")) +
  theme_slide(11) +
  ggplot2::theme(plot.caption = ggplot2::element_text(hjust = 1, colour = "grey45", size = 9,
                                    margin = ggplot2::margin(t = 4)),
        legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "right",
        legend.margin = ggplot2::margin(0, 0, -6, 0),
        legend.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 10, colour = "grey25"),
        panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "grey92"),
        strip.placement = "outside",
        strip.text.y.left = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 0, face = "bold",
                                         colour = ncl_blue, hjust = 1),
        axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "grey25", hjust = 0, size = 8.5),
        panel.spacing.y = grid::unit(0.45, "lines"))
```

::: {.src}
@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne, Figure 3, rebuilt from the published values at osf.io/gvm2z.
:::

::: notes
These are the twenty-nine analyses of one dataset. The odds ratios run from nought point eight nine, which implies that dark-skinned players were red-carded slightly less often, to two point nine three, with a median of one point three one. Twenty of the twenty-nine intervals exclude one and nine do not, so about two thirds of the teams found an effect and a third did not, on identical data. [pause] The left-hand column groups the teams by the distribution of the outcome that they assumed, linear, logistic, Poisson, and two that fit none of the three. Each team took that decision for itself, and each choice was defensible. You take a decision of the same kind yourselves on the specification menu, where the outcome family is one of the choices.
:::

## 'Replication' crises

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Another 'replication' crisis – terminological confusion?
:::
::: {.fragment}
The term 'reproducibility' has been used as a synonym for a number of different characteristics – reproducibility, robustness, replicability, repeatability, credibility, and trustworthiness [@NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms, p. 2].
:::
[[Successfully rerun the same code on the same data?]{colour="#b22222"}]{.fragment}
[[Re-analyse the same data a different way?]{colour="#1C69A8"}]{.fragment}
[[Collect fresh data and analyse it in the same way?]{colour="#4D179A"}]{.fragment}
[[Using the same data and same analysis but asking a different question?]{colour="#3C6301"}]{.fragment}
[[Asking the same question but answering it with fresh data and a different analysis?]{colour="#3BB8DB"}]{.fragment}
::::

::: notes
Twenty-nine competent teams worked on one dataset and did not agree, and I have not yet said what kind of failure that is. Part of the difficulty lies in the word. [advance] For years 'replication' covered rerunning someone's code, reanalysing their data in a different way and collecting new data altogether, three operations that answer three different questions. Because all three were called 'replication', the debates about the crisis had people talking past each other for a decade, so before any more numbers we need the vocabulary. [advance through the five questions]
:::
